extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists and writers preparing/querying agents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and submitting effective agent query letters for novels, emphasizing that the manuscript must be complete, the query should be a proper pitch (not a request for idea validation), and that revision and adherence to submission etiquette matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finished manuscript requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: You have to have a finished novel. There are no exceptions to this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you send a query for an unfinished novel, don't say so. It's bad enough to actually do it, it's worse to say so. The first step for writing a query letter is to finish the novel. QueryShark does not read queries for unfinished novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query letters (not synopses or first pages)
rubrics_metrics.description: The QueryShark blog is a critique of query letters, not synopses or first pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not submit a synopsis or sample pages expecting a query critique; the focus should be on crafting a proper query letter (a concise pitch/presentation), not on submitting manuscript excerpts to this venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query must clearly state what the story is about
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate query should explain what your story is about; a submission that doesn't do this is not a query.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear, concise pitch/hook that tells an agent what the book is about rather than asking strangers whether your idea is worth pursuing. The comment 'Not to mention this isn't actually a query ... What is your story about?' exemplifies this expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise queries thoroughly and use archives/feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Revising query letters based on examples and critiques is essential to improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the QueryShark archives for good and bad examples and revise repeatedly — several commenters and success stories note multiple revisions (sometimes many) before success. Join critique groups (e.g., Critters.org, Backspace) or other communities to get feedback and iterate until the query is polished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow submission guidelines and basic mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhere to submission guidelines and use correct punctuation and grammar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper formatting, punctuation, and grammar matter when submitting queries; following an agent's or blog's submission rules increases your chances and avoids easy rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expect public critique or immediate posting
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a long queue of unposted queries and QueryShark selects queries at random based on what catches the shark's eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of the post, thousands of queries may be waiting. Don't bank on getting posted or getting a reply; use other channels for feedback and be patient. The blog chooses queries that are instructive, unusual, or exemplary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions for unfinished manuscripts are rare and contextual
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions (e.g., works accepted before completion) exist but are uncommon and typically involve prior recognition or personal connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples like Zadie Smith's early deal are atypical and usually occur when the author already has a track record or met an agent in person; cold queries for unfinished manuscripts virtually never succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate channel for private critique
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want a private, not-public critique, use private review services rather than the public QueryShark blog.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog provides public critiques selectively; for guaranteed individual feedback consider paid/private critique options (e.g., TheQueryShark or critique groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't ask strangers to validate whether your idea is 'worth it'
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking strangers whether your idea is good enough to pursue (before completing it) is inappropriate for a query.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing is an act of faith; you can't reliably know if an idea is publishable until you complete it. Seek peer feedback via critique groups instead of cold queries asking for validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure manuscript length and readiness appropriate to genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure the manuscript is sufficiently developed and of an appropriate length for its genre before considering queries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters note that many fantasies routinely go over 100K and that some writers would wait until 30–40K before being confident; the underlying rule is that the manuscript should be a complete, genre-appropriate draft before querying.
